items.title: Vercel Functions now support request bodies up to 20MiB
items.summary: Vercel Functions now accept inbound request bodies up to 20MiB, up from 4.5MB, in Public Beta. To turn this on, set the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1 environment variable. The opt-in applies to the whole project in the environment where you set it, so you can test the larger limit on preview before enabling it in production. It requires the project's functions to use the performance memory setting of 4GB. It applies to functions on the Node.js, Python, and Bun runtimes, and to Routing Middleware. Functions and Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime keep the 4.5MB cap and return 413 on oversize bodies, so moving them onto the larger limit means switching to the Node.js runtime with runtime: 'nodejs' , or proxy.ts in Next.js. When a project opts in, Routing Middleware receives request headers and metadata but no request body, enforced at the project level. Middleware still runs and still sees every other request header, so body-dependent middleware behavior is the one thing that becomes unavailable. This avoids sending the body twice, to both middleware and the target function, which would raise cost and time to first byte. When handling larger request bodies, read the body promptly and avoid holding it in memory to prevent backpressure and memory issues. Learn more in the Vercel Functions limitations documentation .

To turn this on, set the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1 environment variable. The opt-in applies to the whole project in the environment where you set it, so you can test the larger limit on preview before enabling it in production. It requires the project's functions to use the performance memory setting of 4GB. It applies to functions on the Node.js, Python, and Bun runtimes, and to Routing Middleware. Functions and Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime keep the 4.5MB cap and return 413 on oversize bodies, so moving them onto the larger limit means switching to the Node.js runtime with runtime: 'nodejs', or proxy.ts in Next.js.

When a project opts in, Routing Middleware receives request headers and metadata but no request body, enforced at the project level. Middleware still runs and still sees every other request header, so body-dependent middleware behavior is the one thing that becomes unavailable. This avoids sending the body twice, to both middleware and the target function, which would raise cost and time to first byte.

When handling larger request bodies, read the body promptly and avoid holding it in memory to prevent backpressure and memory issues.

Learn more in the Vercel Functions limitations documentation.

items.title: 🚀 AutoGPT Platform v0.12.0
items.summary: ⚠️ Breaking change The frontend no longer reads TRUST_X_FORWARDED_FOR ( #16530 , @Pwuts ). A self-hosted frontend that set it by hand gets no client IP from X-Forwarded-For for the sign-in IP log, IP blocks and per-visitor store search until TRUSTED_PROXIES lists the proxy in front of it. The single-container image and Vercel need nothing. What to do: if your frontend sets TRUST_X_FORWARDED_FOR , remove it and set TRUSTED_PROXIES to a comma-separated list of the addresses or CIDR ranges of the proxies in front of it. Until you do, the frontend logs a warning at start that the old setting is ignored. The same TRUSTED_PROXIES setting now also names the proxies for the backend and the External API's per-address limits, replacing FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS and TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT , which keep working but are deprecated; behind your own reverse proxy, the single-container image takes it too. See Client IP Addresses . ✨ Highlights Get started faster. Signing up takes fewer steps (no more typing your password twice), the sign-up and login pages show up right away, and setup no longer gets stuck on "Loading your setup…". Sign up with Google and you can connect Gmail, Drive and Calendar in the same step. ( #16829 , #16831 , #16968 , #16845 , #16877 ) Safer sign-ins. Adding a new way to sign in to your account (Google, Microsoft, GitHub or Discord) now takes a six-digit code from your inbox, unless that provider runs your mailbox (Gmail through Google, Outlook.com through Microsoft). You also get an email whenever a new sign-in method is added. ( #16860 ) Never lose a message. If Otto can't confirm your message arrived, one click on Send again delivers it, files included, without sending it twice. And "Thinking…" now stays up until Otto starts answering, so you always know it's working. ( #17041 , #16962 , #17038 ) Always see where your runs really are. After a brief connection drop, your Library, run history, Activity and chats catch up on their own, so a run that already finished no longer looks like it's still going. Live updates also keep flowing on slow connections. ( #16898 , #16915 , #16932 , #16903 , #16865 , #16960 ) Schedules you can count on. During brief maintenance your schedules show as temporarily unavailable instead of disappearing, a run that comes due during a restart still runs (exactly once), and retrying a schedule you just created no longer makes a duplicate. ( #16937 , #16866 , #16919 , #16904 ) More models to choose from. Gemini 4 Neon, GPT-6.2 Astra, GPT-6.2 Sol and Qwen 4 Max are now available in your workflows, and Otto's advanced Codex tier now runs on GPT-6.2 Astra. ( #17023 , #16870 , #16899 , #16836 , #16852 , #16902 ) More tools for Otto. Otto can now connect to AnySearch, Supabase, Klaviyo, AI/ML API and CompanyEnrich, reads from Supabase no longer need your approval each time, and Otto now finds the custom MCP servers you've connected by URL. ( #16913 , #16659 , #16850 , #15202 , #16771 , #16447 , #15168 ) Work in progress: AutoGPT in your pocket. Our new native mobile app puts your team on your phone: sign in, chat with Otto and your experts, hire experts from the Marketplace, connect your services right from the chat, and talk instead of typing with live voice dictation. ( #16715 , #16869 , #16923 , #17058 ) 🔒 Security This release fixes several privately reported security issues. We'll publish the advisories once the fixes are live in production. 🧩 Also in this release Otto and AutoPilot Experts hired from chat or the API introduce themselves ( #16687 , @Bentlybro ) Measure first answer timing separately from model activity ( #15533 , @ntindle ) Measure send-to-answer timing in chat ( #15541 , @ntindle ) Let the greeting's Sonnet call think, so OpenRouter stops refusing ⚠️ Breaking change

The frontend no longer reads TRUST_X_FORWARDED_FOR (#16530, @Pwuts). A self-hosted frontend that set it by hand gets no client IP from X-Forwarded-For for the sign-in IP log, IP blocks and per-visitor store search until TRUSTED_PROXIES lists the proxy in front of it. The single-container image and Vercel need nothing.

What to do: if your frontend sets TRUST_X_FORWARDED_FOR, remove it and set TRUSTED_PROXIES to a comma-separated list of the addresses or CIDR ranges of the proxies in front of it. Until you do, the frontend logs a warning at start that the old setting is ignored. The same TRUSTED_PROXIES setting now also names the proxies for the backend and the External API's per-address limits, replacing FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS and TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT, which keep working but are deprecated; behind your own reverse proxy, the single-container image takes it too. See Client IP Addresses.

✨ Highlights
  • Get started faster. Signing up takes fewer steps (no more typing your password twice), the sign-up and login pages show up right away, and setup no longer gets stuck on "Loading your setup…". Sign up with Google and you can connect Gmail, Drive and Calendar in the same step. (#16829, #16831, #16968, #16845, #16877)
  • Safer sign-ins. Adding a new way to sign in to your account (Google, Microsoft, GitHub or Discord) now takes a six-digit code from your inbox, unless that provider runs your mailbox (Gmail through Google, Outlook.com through Microsoft). You also get an email whenever a new sign-in method is added. (#16860)
  • Never lose a message. If Otto can't confirm your message arrived, one click on Send again delivers it, files included, without sending it twice. And "Thinking…" now stays up until Otto starts answering, so you always know it's working. (#17041, #16962, #17038)
  • Always see where your runs really are. After a brief connection drop, your Library, run history, Activity and chats catch up on their own, so a run that already finished no longer looks like it's still going. Live updates also keep flowing on slow connections. (#16898, #16915, #16932, #16903, #16865, #16960)
  • Schedules you can count on. During brief maintenance your schedules show as temporarily unavailable instead of disappearing, a run that comes due during a restart still runs (exactly once), and retrying a schedule you just created no longer makes a duplicate. (#16937, #16866, #16919, #16904)
  • More models to choose from. Gemini 4 Neon, GPT-6.2 Astra, GPT-6.2 Sol and Qwen 4 Max are now available in your workflows, and Otto's advanced Codex tier now runs on GPT-6.2 Astra. (#17023, #16870, #16899, #16836, #16852, #16902)
  • More tools for Otto. Otto can now connect to AnySearch, Supabase, Klaviyo, AI/ML API and CompanyEnrich, reads from Supabase no longer need your approval each time, and Otto now finds the custom MCP servers you've connected by URL. (#16913, #16659, #16850, #15202, #16771, #16447, #15168)

Work in progress:

  • AutoGPT in your pocket. Our new native mobile app puts your team on your phone: sign in, chat with Otto and your experts, hire experts from the Marketplace, connect your services right from the chat, and talk instead of typing with live voice dictation. (#16715, #16869, #16923, #17058)
🔒 Security

This release fixes several privately reported security issues. We'll publish the advisories once the fixes are live in production.

🧩 Also in this release Otto and AutoPilot
  • Experts hired from chat or the API introduce themselves (#16687, @Bentlybro)
  • Measure first answer timing separately from model activity (#15533, @ntindle)
  • Measure send-to-answer timing in chat (#15541, @ntindle)
  • Let the greeting's Sonnet call think, so OpenRouter stops refusing it (#16781, @Pwuts)
  • Reword the Founder plan's third task reason (#16851, @kcze)
  • Tell Otto a refused tool call did not happen (#17036, @kcze)
  • Judge a failed tool's error text like its output (#16884, @ntindle)
  • bash_exec says when a command killed its own shell (#16347, @Pwuts)
  • List nested block output objects by field name in describe_capability (#16679, @Bentlybro)
  • Keep saved file names in the bot's reply text (#16680, @Bentlybro)
  • Don't create a second schedule for work already scheduled (#16678, @Bentlybro)
  • Consume an approval at most once (#16863, @ntindle)
  • Refund a block run whose saved review can't be read (#16895, @ntindle)
  • Back off sub-agent catch-ups while stale, and close two pub/sub gaps (#16888, @ntindle)
  • Scope find_session and message_session to the calling chat's organization (#16966, @ntindle)
  • find_session and message_session read sessions over RPC (#16858, @ntindle)
  • Keep a chat's skill index for 15 minutes so follow-ups stop rebuilding it (#15985, @ntindle)
  • Start a message's paywall and in-flight reads beside its session checks (#15779, @ntindle)
  • Read an expert's row beside its owner's scope in the turn's check (#15854, @ntindle)
  • Save a chat message without re-reading its session or its next sequence (#15486, @ntindle)
  • Save a chat message and its session's fields in one transaction (#15987, @ntindle)
Builder and workflows
  • Ctrl/Cmd+Z in a builder text field undoes the text, not the workflow (#17035, @kcze)
  • Save the builder graph from one loaded snapshot after a save (#17021, @ntindle)
  • A stored review decision wins over safe mode (#16874, @ntindle)
  • Look up a node's waiting run with a correlated query, so a busy pin name can't time it out (#16835, @Pwuts)
  • Scope four workflow and run routes to the request's organization (#16931, @Pwuts)
  • Expand Unix cron day-of-week tokens to day sets before APS mapping (#15321, @ntindle)
  • Bound custom cron intervals so APScheduler accepts them (#15322, @ntindle)
Integrations and blocks
  • Group Parallel Search MCP with native Parallel provider (#16572, @Iitian001)
  • Surface regex errors in Extract Text Information; forward falsy data in Match Text Pattern (#15313, @ntindle)
  • Read Spreadsheet handles short, ragged, duplicate-header and blank-line CSVs (#15317, @ntindle)
  • Short block input error messages (#17000, @kcze)
Platform and self-hosting
  • Boxes behind the swap proxy trust its signing CA (#16627, @kcze)
  • Refuse uploads clamd can't scan whole instead of scanning them in pieces; the bundled ClamAV's limits rise to 256M (#16694, @ntindle)
  • Resume a streamed download where storage ended early, and stop gzip holding it back (#16838, @Pwuts)
  • Harden credential masking in validation logs and error reports (#16956, @ntindle)
  • Keep request credentials out of error reports and logs (#16908, @ntindle)
  • Admin requeue publishes stuck QUEUED executions (#15328, @ntindle)
  • Report memory graph truncation only when something was cut (#16762, @67-luck)
Other fixes
  • Show a failed trial's Pay now button by reading its subscription with the card expanded (#16834, @Pwuts)
  • Prevent translation extensions from breaking suggested tasks on Home (#16776, @sentry[bot])
  • Stop the avatar image hang and drop networkidle waits from e2e (#17013, @ntindle)

Dependencies: 5 bumps (#16945, #16943, #16944, #16946, #16947).

CI, tests and developer tooling: 11 changes (#17012, #16799, #16832, #16918, #16842, #16924, #16914, #16930, #16876, #16859, #16928).

Documentation: 3 changes (#17002, #16892, #16519).

@ntindle, @Bentlybro, @67-luck, @Pwuts, @kcze, @Lookoff-AIMLAPI, @Iitian001, @namirali, @ayush-singh-0601, @0ubbe

items.title: Vercel completes ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification
items.summary: Vercel has completed its ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, meeting the international standard for AI management systems. This certification gives our customers confidence to ship fast with agents on Vercel, demonstrating how Vercel designs, builds, operates, and governs our AI products. Our AI management system covers Vercel’s underlying infrastructure and core AI products, including AI Gateway, Vercel Agent, v0, AI-based open source software and frameworks, as well as the people and processes behind them. Vercel’s certificate is available here , and additional audit documentation is available through our Trust Center . What is ISO 42001? ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard for AI management systems and applies to any organization that develops, provides, or uses AI. An AI management system is the set of policies, roles, processes, and controls through which an organization consistently governs AI activities. The standard includes requirements for leadership accountability, AI risk assessment, lifecycle management, data governance, transparency, and continual improvement. The requirement that makes ISO 42001 distinct from security standards is the AI system impact assessment. Security frameworks cover how an organization protects information, but ISO 42001 covers how it builds and uses AI, including the assessment of how an AI system impacts the people it touches, and the benefits and harms that would result when that system materially changes. To obtain the certification, we underwent a two-stage audit performed by an independent, accredited certification body, which evaluated whether our AI management system is designed correctly and operates effectively. The certificate is valid for three years, with annual surveillance audits in between. “Enterprises want agents in production, but no one should have to choose between moving fast with AI and governing it well,” said Talha Tariq, CTO for Security. “We built our AI governance to run as continuously as we ship, and ISO 42001 is the independent check that it works.” What this means for customers AI moved into the critical path of how software gets built faster than the governance around it did. Teams are shipping agents, assistants, and model-backed features on Vercel every day, and the questions that follow are no longer hypothetical: Who is accountable when a model behaves unexpectedly? What data reached a model? How is the system monitored once it’s live? Who decided the system was ready? We pursued ISO 42001 because we are committed to providing enterprise-grade AI products. This certification attests that we run deliberate, auditable AI systems. How we govern AI at Vercel There are three primary ways AI is governed at Vercel. Impact assessments Vercel conducts AI system impact assessments which cover foreseeable benefits, harms, failures, and misuse. We reassess these risks and benefits when the system materially changes. Evaluations before release We maintain evals for our AI systems covering performance, safety, and security, with human review for material changes. Clear data commitments Where it is not the default option based on pricing plan, we provide customers the ability to set their data handling preferences ranging from zero data retention (ZDR) to training opt-out. Our AI policy is available at v0.app/policy. Ship fast, with confidence We are committed to helping teams ship fast with confidence in the way AI is built and governed at Vercel. ISO 42001 is proof of that commitment, giving our customers: Confidence in agentic infrastructure: Vercel’s AI systems have been audited, which means customers using our AI products start from a reviewed foundation instead of an unexamined one. Governance can ship at the speed of the product: Agents now drive the development and deployment of applications. Governance and oversight that occurs quarterly can’t govern software that changes hourly, so we built a system that reviews AI as continuously as we ship it. Simplified and accelerated assurance: Customers and partners can rely on this certification, alongside our other compliance attestations, to meet AI governance diligence requirements for faster third-party vendor onboarding. Clear lines of responsibility: ISO 42001 requires that responsibilities be allocated across the AI supply chain. Our documentation outlines what Vercel is accountable for and what remains yours, the same shared-responsibility model we use for security. Discipline that holds over time: Annual surveillance audits mean this isn’t a one-time claim. As our AI products change, the system that governs them stays under independent review. AI is changing what people build on Vercel, and we intend for the governance around it to keep pace. We’ll continue to expand the scope of our certifications as our products grow.

Vercel has completed its ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, meeting the international standard for AI management systems.

This certification gives our customers confidence to ship fast with agents on Vercel, demonstrating how Vercel designs, builds, operates, and governs our AI products.

Our AI management system covers Vercel’s underlying infrastructure and core AI products, including AI Gateway, Vercel Agent, v0, AI-based open source software and frameworks, as well as the people and processes behind them.

Vercel’s certificate is available here, and additional audit documentation is available through our Trust Center.

What is ISO 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard for AI management systems and applies to any organization that develops, provides, or uses AI.

An AI management system is the set of policies, roles, processes, and controls through which an organization consistently governs AI activities. The standard includes requirements for leadership accountability, AI risk assessment, lifecycle management, data governance, transparency, and continual improvement.

The requirement that makes ISO 42001 distinct from security standards is the AI system impact assessment. Security frameworks cover how an organization protects information, but ISO 42001 covers how it builds and uses AI, including the assessment of how an AI system impacts the people it touches, and the benefits and harms that would result when that system materially changes.

To obtain the certification, we underwent a two-stage audit performed by an independent, accredited certification body, which evaluated whether our AI management system is designed correctly and operates effectively. The certificate is valid for three years, with annual surveillance audits in between.

“Enterprises want agents in production, but no one should have to choose between moving fast with AI and governing it well,” said Talha Tariq, CTO for Security. “We built our AI governance to run as continuously as we ship, and ISO 42001 is the independent check that it works.”

What this means for customers

AI moved into the critical path of how software gets built faster than the governance around it did. Teams are shipping agents, assistants, and model-backed features on Vercel every day, and the questions that follow are no longer hypothetical:

  • Who is accountable when a model behaves unexpectedly?

  • What data reached a model?

  • How is the system monitored once it’s live?

  • Who decided the system was ready?

We pursued ISO 42001 because we are committed to providing enterprise-grade AI products. This certification attests that we run deliberate, auditable AI systems.

How we govern AI at Vercel

There are three primary ways AI is governed at Vercel.

Impact assessments

Vercel conducts AI system impact assessments which cover foreseeable benefits, harms, failures, and misuse. We reassess these risks and benefits when the system materially changes.

Evaluations before release

We maintain evals for our AI systems covering performance, safety, and security, with human review for material changes.

Clear data commitments

Where it is not the default option based on pricing plan, we provide customers the ability to set their data handling preferences ranging from zero data retention (ZDR) to training opt-out. Our AI policy is available at v0.app/policy.

Ship fast, with confidence

We are committed to helping teams ship fast with confidence in the way AI is built and governed at Vercel. ISO 42001 is proof of that commitment, giving our customers:

  • Confidence in agentic infrastructure: Vercel’s AI systems have been audited, which means customers using our AI products start from a reviewed foundation instead of an unexamined one.

  • Governance can ship at the speed of the product: Agents now drive the development and deployment of applications. Governance and oversight that occurs quarterly can’t govern software that changes hourly, so we built a system that reviews AI as continuously as we ship it.

  • Simplified and accelerated assurance: Customers and partners can rely on this certification, alongside our other compliance attestations, to meet AI governance diligence requirements for faster third-party vendor onboarding.

  • Clear lines of responsibility: ISO 42001 requires that responsibilities be allocated across the AI supply chain. Our documentation outlines what Vercel is accountable for and what remains yours, the same shared-responsibility model we use for security.

  • Discipline that holds over time: Annual surveillance audits mean this isn’t a one-time claim. As our AI products change, the system that governs them stays under independent review.

AI is changing what people build on Vercel, and we intend for the governance around it to keep pace. We’ll continue to expand the scope of our certifications as our products grow.

items.title: Ask HN: Does AI slop require more marketing in the future?
items.summary: Now that after Anthropic's IPO debut and with OpenAPI IPO in the works there is no doubt that the % of AI slop is going to increase disproportionately though this study says it has indeed gone down in 2026 since 2025 (https://tom-riley.co.uk/blog/ai-generated-content-statistics/) [The study itself seems to be an AI slop?] . An analysis of 100 companies highlighted on YouTube found that while AI generated content accounted for 52.1% of published material, it generated only 4.9% of organic traffic. Meanwhile, original human content made up just 14.5% of volume but captured 87% of the traffic. If this is the case then how can AI labs generate revenue? Even if we assume that the AI slop is going to raise after the IPOs, the content market is going to shrink and it will dilute the revenue for the content creators (using AI) forcing them to start marketing their AI slop to get visibility in the market. This is a very interesting trend to watch out for. When I say AI slop content I am not meaning just about web publishing (Web slop), but also synthetic vibe coding (Code slop), data analysis (Data slop), agentic workflow (Software Engineering slop) etc. If there are 1000 of the same kind of software/app clones (of course vibe coded) which will you buy? How does this compete with the originally human architected, designed and developed software/app? Finally I think it comes down to trust. Please share your thoughts.

items.title: Show HN: GhostFleet: A Battleship game with an advanced AI opponent
items.summary: Hi HN I've always been drawn to puzzle and strategy games, and for a long time I've wanted to build a game of my own. While building my own version of battleship, I came across this idea of adding a super intelligent in-game AI which uses probability and statistics to reason with the board and fire its next shot. The goal was to create a set of rules & logic capable of consistently outperforming human players, much like chess engines that have evolved to surpass even the world's strongest human chess players. Thus I created WraithAI and named the game as Ghostfleet. WraithAI features: 1. Monte Carlo Simulation with Probability heatmaps: Before every turn WraithAI samples 800 possible enemy fleet configurations and aggregates them into a probability heatmap. It identifies the most likely locations of the enemy ships. 2. Bayesian Inference: After every shot it updates its beliefs and uses the information gain to draw a new heatmap. When two cells look equally likely WraithAI picks the one whose result would tell more about the hidden enemy fleet for its next turn. 3. Adaptive Strategy & defense: It adjusts its aggression based on the state of the game and has a mechanism which resists common search strategies. I would genuinely like to know how people can find patterns in its behavior. Can you outsmart & beat WraithAI? Ghostfleet also has multiplayer mode so you can play with your friends. There is a matchmaking component called TownSquare at the bottom through which you can share room codes with other players. You can play directly in your browser: 1. Play against WraithAI: https://ghostfleet.in/play?mode=wraithAI 2. Ghostfleet: https://ghostfleet.in/ 3. WraithAI Technical breakdown: https://ghostfleet.in/wraith-ai

items.title: Preview seed fixture (rolling)
items.summary: Rolling, fully SYNTHETIC preview-database seed fixture baked from dev@9c2d9e1a523b (migration head: 20261112120000_account_deletion_confirmation_skipped). Preview environments restore fixture.dump.gz (custom-format, gzipped, platform schema only, including _prisma_migrations) BEFORE running a PR's own migrations, so schema changes run against populated tables. RESTORE: apply restore-preamble.sql to the target database first (it creates the platform schema and installs the vector + pg_trgm extensions into it, which pg_dump --schema=platform omits), then run 'gunzip -c fixture.dump.gz | pg_restore -d --no-owner' WITHOUT --exit-on-error (the dump's own CREATE SCHEMA collides benignly with the preamble's). SECURITY INVARIANT: this bake holds no cloud credentials and has no read path to any real database — it runs entirely against a throwaway Postgres container and contains only synthetic rows (Faker-generated, plus the hand-written preview marketplace) and the already-public marketplace agent exports checked into autogpt_platform/backend/agents/. This asset is regenerated on every eligible dev push and weekly; treat it as disposable.

items.title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
items.summary: Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning! You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YlkIc3L29lo A (somewhat long) summary: When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways. Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio. Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said. The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails. More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls. Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call. For audio misunderstandings, we run multiple, even numerous, transcription models on most calls, giving more “shots on goal” from the original audio. Even if none gets it exactly right, multiple almost-correct answers let us triangulate on a correct transcript, using one or more LLMs to decide what the caller actually said. In challenging situations, we even pipe caller audio directly to one or more audio-input LLMs to further improve comprehension. For instruction following, we run a mix of fast and slow LLMs on conversation turns to combine snappy responses with deeper thinking behind the scenes. In practice, this is a multi-staged classification problem: after 50ms, 500ms, 1s, etc., we simultaneously generate responses with increasing inference while classifying whether we need to “think harder” to generate a definitive correct answer. Together with other smaller optimizations, these two approaches have been very effective. Qualitatively, customer calls go much more smoothly and reach successful outcomes far more frequently than on three-step or speech-to-speech pipelines. Quantitatively, we’ve set a record of 99.4% on the Big Bench Audio benchmark, smarter than any other model fast enough for real calls. (We’re also benchmarking ThunderPhone on more public benchmarks - stay tuned.) The downside is configuration complexity. Every agent benefits from a different setup on the ThunderPhone stack, and even individual call turns on the same call often benefit from different stacks. Configuring this manually worked for enterprise customers, but made it prohibitive to give smaller self-serve customers the full benefits without giving their agents our full attention. That’s how Zeus came about. Our enterprise configurations were repetitive enough that an AI could do them once we taught it how and gave it the right tools. We’re big fans of Claude Code and Codex for software development, but they fall short at configuring voice agents for a few reasons. First, unlike software development, where you can compile code and run tests to verify things work, you can’t run live calls inside a computer right after configuring a voice agent - and coding agents don’t know how to run simulated calls out of the box, or “listen” to a call to spot real problems. We built both capabilities into Zeus, giving it a “closed loop” experience building, testing, and improving voice agents just like coding agents have with regular software. Second, coding agents are pretty gullible about marketing claims. Companies building AI and voice infrastructure commonly post the most favorable possible interpretation of their capabilities online. Claude and Codex read those claims, believe them uncritically, and pick tools based on marketing rather than real performance. At best, that leads to suboptimal architectural choices; at worst, to voice agents that don’t really work at all. We’ve sidestepped this with continuous evals feeding an internal knowledge base. For everything that matters for voice agents - accurate audio understanding, instruction following, noise cancelling, turn-taking, and more - we maintain internal benchmarks built on real call data. Every time a new AI model comes out, we (now mostly automatically) feed it through our evals for performance, speed, cost, and reliability/consistency. That feeds our internal knowledge base, which Zeus uses to pick the right stack for every agent, call, and conversation turn. This all happens behind the scenes to keep the ThunderPhone experience seamless. A user just describes their use case and goals, and Zeus helps fill in ambiguities, connect VoIP and software integrations, and optimize the voice agent(s) on simulated and live calls until they hit the highest performance on business goals (conversions, unit economics, etc.) possible with today’s models. Zeus is also differentiated on cost. Zeus itself is free to use for now, though we expect to move to subscription or token-based pricing later. For calls, we’ve become the first voice AI vendor to our knowledge to charge on a cost-plus basis: ThunderPhone customers pay exactly what we pay our vendors, plus a 17% margin on calls costing 2c/min or less, scaling linearly up to 25% for calls costing us 15c/min or more, and 25% from there on up. However, we find that simple phone agents do well on a stack that costs about 2c/min, and more complex cases typically land around 5-10c/min - significantly cheaper than most alternatives. Zeus is brand-new, so we’re eager to get feedback on how it works for customers, and any areas we could improve it. Give it a try and see what you think - let me know if you have any feedback or questions. Alex
